title: The default branch is the main path
statement: When most learners carry no placement or mastery signal, design a routing plan's default branch as its main path and check it doesn't hold everyone back.
example: In one grade, 1,389 of 1,640 learners (85%) had neither a placement nor a mastery signal.
detail: A feasibility red team on a second-grade reading redesign queried the grade and found 1,389 of 1,640 learners (85%) with neither a placement nor a mastery signal, so the plan's no-signal fallback was the common case, not an edge case (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/redteam-3-feasibility.md`, lines 218-219). It asked the design to justify routing 85% of a grade through a conservative path by default and to show that path doesn't become a universal speed bump (the same file, lines 222-223). A setup review of the same grade concluded that course-entry logic must assume no internal signal as the default branch, since the minority with one was a strong-skewed sample (`grade3-reading/ti-courseplans/courses/g2-reading/analysis/g2-reading-setup-layers.md`, lines 50-52).

evidence.quote: **1,640 G2 students; 1,389 (85%) have neither a placement nor a mastery signal.** So the default branch isn't an edge case — **~85% of students hit it.**
the design must justify routing 85% of a grade through a conservative path by default without walling — and prove the on-ramp doesn't become a universal speed-bump.
you cannot place G2 students off internal mastery for ~82% of the grade, and the 18% you *can* is a biased (strong-skewed) sample.
Any course-entry logic must assume "no internal signal" as the default branch.
